provenance: IBM AMLworld HI-Small (Altman et al., Kaggle ealtman2019/ibm-transactions-for-anti-money-laundering-aml, CDLA-Sharing-1.0). The corpus is entirely SYNTHETIC by IBM's own statement -- generated by a multi-agent virtual world, not real customer data. An earlier revision of this line opened with the word 'real' and then said synthetic in its next sentence; what is real is the provenance, not the transactions. These are unmodified rows of the published corpus, carrying the engineered features finance_aml.gbm was actually trained on, unlike the 8-feature PaySim sample this page uses for the FHE/MPC pipeline. Z-scored here by the StandardScaler published in the student's weights.json -- the same transform it was distilled under. These are the identical rows the gradient-boosting teacher's sample ships, so the two numbers on this page describe one row set.

input.layout: samples[i] is one transaction's 32 engineered features, z-scored

expected.note: 0.4865 on THESE rows, which is not the 0.0614 the registry records for this student. That figure is measured on the full 1,523,504-row test split at AMLworld's real prevalence of about 1 in 981; these 8192 rows are stratified to contain positives, because an unstratified draw of that corpus is all-negative and every metric on it is vacuous. Rare-class F1 rises with prevalence, so the two differ by about 19x and neither is wrong. What survives the change is the ratio to the all-positive baseline: 13.6x here against roughly 8.7x on the full corpus. Read this number against the 0.0357 baseline beside it, not against the registry's.
